792.title: Nala and Damayanti
792.hook: Damayanti wakes alone in half a cloth, and walks through the forest asking mountains and trees for her husband
792.howItsDone: Damayanti's wandering, from the forest to the court of Chedi, is told in the Nala story of the Mahabharata's Vana Parva, where her lament to the Ashoka tree plays on the tree's name, 'without sorrow'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nala and Damayanti shared one cloth in the forest, until he cut it in the dark and left. Who did you notice staying beside you? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

Half a cloth. That's what Damayanti finds when she wakes on the floor of the empty rest house. Half of the garment they shared, and no husband. She calls his name. She runs through the trees calling it, half thinking he's hiding, playing some cruel game. Come out, she says, I'm frightened. Nobody answers. Only the trees, and the empty road, and her own voice coming back. And the story, which has followed Nala until now, turns and follows her.
screen: `HALF A CLOTH.` → `SHE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `THE STORY FOLLOWS HER.`

segments.voice: Her first thought, the story says, is for him: who will look after him now, hungry and alone in the forest? Then the forest closes in. A huge serpent seizes her, and even in its coils she cries out for Nala, not for herself. A hunter hears her, kills the snake and frees her. Then he looks at her the wrong way. She sees what he intends. And Damayanti, who has nothing, no husband, no clothes, no kingdom, still has the force of her own faithfulness. In the story it's enough. She curses him, and the hunter falls dead. Then she walks. And as she walks, she talks to everything. She asks a mountain whether it has seen a king named Nala. She meets a group of ascetics who tell her she'll see Nala again, and then they vanish, hermitage and all. She comes to an Ashoka tree in bloom, and the tree's name means without sorrow, and she asks it to live up to its name: take my sorrow, tell me where he went. The tree doesn't answer. She joins a band of traveling merchants. In the night, wild elephants crash through their camp, and in the morning some of the survivors look at the strange half-dressed woman and wonder aloud whether she brought them bad luck. At last she comes to the city of Chedi, ragged, and the queen mother sees her from a window and takes her in. Damayanti agrees to serve, on her own terms: she will keep her dignity, and she won't speak with men who come seeking her. Look at her. She lost the same things Nala lost, and then she lost Nala too. But she never stops asking where he is.
screen: `THE SERPENT AND THE HUNTER.` · `SHE ASKS A MOUNTAIN.` · `"ASHOKA, TAKE MY SORROW."` · then, large: `SHE NEVER STOPS ASKING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Damayanti spoke to the mountains and the trees because there was no one else to tell. Choose one thing near you that's been there through a hard season: a window, a plant, a mug, a street outside. Rest your eyes on it, or picture it. Breathe in. Breathe out. Let it be a quiet witness for a moment, without asking anything of it. If you pray, you can bring whatever you've been carrying into your prayer. If not, simply let the thing in front of you keep you company. The bell holds the time.
Nala and Damayanti. Today, Damayanti alone: a serpent, a hunter, an Ashoka tree, a caravan, a city, and one question asked of everything she meets.
Your line: Nala and Damayanti. Today, keep asking the one question that matters to you, even if nothing answers yet. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

793.title: Nala and Damayanti
793.hook: Nala carries a snake out of a forest fire, and its bite hides him from the world
793.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's Nala story, the serpent Karkotaka disguises Nala and sends him to serve King Rituparna as the charioteer Vahuka, while Damayanti, back in Vidarbha, sends Brahmanas to search for him.

segments.voice: Yesterday the story of Nala and Damayanti followed her alone, asking a mountain and an Ashoka tree where he'd gone. What question did you keep asking? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

A voice in a forest fire. Nala, wandering alone after leaving Damayanti, hears someone calling his name out of the flames. Come quickly, Nala. He follows the voice and finds, curled in the fire, a great serpent. It's Karkotaka, a king among the nagas, and he can't move: a sage's curse has frozen him there until Nala comes to carry him. So the man who lost everything at dice lifts a snake king onto his shoulder and walks out of the fire. And then the snake bites him.
screen: `A VOICE IN THE FIRE.` → `KARKOTAKA, THE SERPENT KING.` → `THEN THE SNAKE BITES HIM.`

segments.voice: Nala's body changes. His beauty is gone. His shape is changed, misshapen, someone no one would look at twice. And Karkotaka explains: I did this so no one will know you. And my poison won't hurt you. It will torment the one who lives inside you, the one who brought all this on you. That's Kali. The bite is a disguise and a medicine at once. Then the serpent gives him a plan. Go to King Rituparna of Ayodhya. Call yourself Vahuka. Offer to drive his horses, because you know horses better than anyone at his court will. And Rituparna knows the secret of dice; he'll teach it to you in exchange. Karkotaka gives him a garment, too: when you want your own shape back, put this on and think of me. So Nala becomes Vahuka, the king's charioteer. He's very good at it. But every evening he says the same lines aloud, a lament for a woman left alone in the forest, wondering where she is. Another servant asks who she is. Nala answers with a story about some foolish man who abandoned his wife, and doesn't say the man is him. Meanwhile, far away, a Brahmana from Vidarbha has found Damayanti at the court of Chedi, and she has gone home to her father's house and her children. She isn't waiting for news. She sends Brahmanas out across the land, to repeat one question in every court and marketplace: where did you go, gambler, after you cut your loving wife's cloth and left her sleeping? And one day, in Ayodhya, a charioteer named Vahuka hears the question, and answers it.
screen: `THE BITE THAT HIDES HIM.` · `NALA BECOMES VAHUKA.` · `A LAMENT EVERY EVENING.` · then, large: `DAMAYANTI SENDS OUT A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle on its own. Nala hides inside a new shape, but every evening the same words come out of him. Notice what your own mind returns to when you're quiet. Don't chase it, and don't push it away. Just let it be there, the way a familiar sound is there in the background of a room. Breathe in, and notice. Breathe out, and let it be. If you pray, you can bring that returning thought into your prayer. If not, simply sit with it kindly. The bell holds the time.
Nala and Damayanti. A snake's bite that hides him and torments Kali, a king become Vahuka the charioteer, and a question sent across the land to find him.
Your line: Nala and Damayanti. Today, notice the words you say to yourself at day's end, and what they're asking for. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

794.title: Nala and Damayanti
794.hook: Damayanti announces a swayamvara for tomorrow, and only one charioteer could get a king there in time
794.howItsDone: The Nala story closes in the Vana Parva with Nala and Damayanti reunited and Nala's kingdom restored; the sage Brihadashva then gives Yudhishthira the knowledge of dice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nala and Damayanti were far apart: he hidden as Vahuka the charioteer, she at home sending out a question. What did you notice yourself saying at day's end? Day seven hundred ninety-four.

The answer comes back to Vidarbha. A charioteer in Ayodhya, misshapen, unremarkable, heard Damayanti's question and answered it with a defense of a husband who had lost even his cloth to the birds. Nobody but Nala would know that. So Damayanti sets a trap made of love. She sends word to King Rituparna: Damayanti is choosing a husband again, and the ceremony is tomorrow. Only a driver like Nala could get a king there in time. If Rituparna arrives, she'll know who drove him.
screen: `THE ANSWER COMES BACK.` → `A SWAYAMVARA, TOMORROW.` → `A TRAP MADE OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Rituparna calls Vahuka, and Nala's heart sinks. Would she really do this? But he harnesses the horses and drives, so fast the king's upper cloth blows away and Vahuka won't stop for it. On the way, Rituparna shows off a gift of his own. He glances at a Vibhitaka tree and tells Vahuka exactly how many leaves and fruits are on it. Vahuka stops, cuts it down, counts, and the king is right. So they trade. Rituparna teaches Nala the secret of the dice, and Nala promises to teach him the secret of horses. And the moment Nala knows the dice, Kali comes out of him. He leaves Nala's body, spitting out Karkotaka's poison, and slips into the Vibhitaka tree. The story says Nala could have cursed him, and doesn't. They reach Vidarbha, and there's no ceremony, no crowd of kings. Damayanti hears the thunder of the chariot and knows the hand on the reins. She sends her maid Keshini to watch the charioteer, and the maid comes back with strange news: low doorways rise for him, empty jars fill when he looks at them. Then Damayanti sends their children to him, and the charioteer weeps. When they finally meet, he asks how she could choose another husband, and she tells him it was only ever a way to find him. A voice from the sky confirms she's been faithful. Nala puts on the serpent's garment and is himself again. Later he wins his kingdom back from Pushkara at dice, and lets his brother go in peace. And in the forest, the sage finishes, and gives Yudhishthira the secret of dice too.
screen: `THE RIDE TO VIDARBHA.` · `THE TREE AND THE SECRET OF DICE.` · `KALI LEAVES NALA.` · then, large: `"IT WAS A WAY TO FIND YOU."`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go. This whole story turns on recognition: Damayanti knows Nala by his answer, by the sound of a chariot, by his tears over their children. Bring to mind someone who knows you that way, who would know you in any disguise. Breathe in, and let yourself be known. Breathe out, and picture the small sign they'd know you by: a laugh, a walk, the way you sign a note. If no one comes to mind, simply rest with the breath. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Nala and Damayanti. Lost at dice, parted in the forest, found again by a question, a fast chariot and a wife who knew his hand on the reins.

795.title: Savitri and Satyavan
795.hook: a king's daughter is so radiant no one dares ask for her, so her father sends her out to choose for herself
795.howItsDone: The story of Savitri and Satyavan is told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira in the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, and Savitri is remembered in Hindu observance, including the Vat Savitri vrata kept by some married women.

segments.voice: Yesterday ended the story of Nala and Damayanti: a trap made of love, a racing chariot, and Kali leaving at last. Who would know you in any disguise? Day seven hundred ninety-five.

Still in the forest, Yudhishthira has another question, this time for the sage Markandeya. He has watched Draupadi suffer beside him through all of it, the hall, the exile, the forest. Has there ever been a woman as devoted as she is? Markandeya answers the way Brihadashva did. With a story. There was a princess, he says, named Savitri. And her story, like Nala's, starts long before the trouble does, with a father who wanted a child.
screen: `ANOTHER QUESTION IN THE FOREST.` → `MARKANDEYA TELLS A STORY.` → `A PRINCESS NAMED SAVITRI.`

segments.voice: Ashvapati, king of the Madras, is good, generous and childless. So he takes up a discipline: he eats sparingly, keeps his senses in check, and makes offerings with the Savitri mantra, for a long time. At last the goddess Savitri herself rises out of the sacred fire and grants him a daughter. He names the girl after the goddess who gave her. Savitri grows up so radiant that people compare her to a goddess. And here the story takes an unexpected turn. Because she is so splendid, no man dares to ask for her hand. The radiance that should draw suitors keeps them away. Her father is troubled. And he does something unusual. He tells her: go yourself. Find a husband worthy of you, and tell me who he is. So Savitri sets out in a chariot, with her father's old counselors beside her, and travels through forests and hermitages, looking. When she comes home, the sage Narada happens to be sitting with her father. Ashvapati asks her where she has been. And Savitri tells them. There is a king of the Shalvas named Dyumatsena, she says. He lost his sight, and an enemy took his kingdom, and now he lives in a forest hermitage with his wife and his son. That son is Satyavan. He's the one I've chosen in my heart. Notice who does the choosing here. It's the daughter, and it isn't a ceremony in a hall. She has gone out into the world and come back with a name. And sitting at the king's side, Narada has heard it. He's about to speak.
screen: `A FATHER'S LONG DISCIPLINE.` · `TOO RADIANT TO BE ASKED.` · `"GO AND CHOOSE FOR YOURSELF."` · then, large: `SHE COMES HOME WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath slow. Savitri went out and looked for herself. Bring to mind one choice in your life that was truly your own, large or small: a friend, a path, a place, a word you said. Breathe in, and let yourself remember choosing it. Breathe out, and let it be what it is, without grading it. If other choices come to mind, the ones made for you, let them pass for now. If you pray, you can bring that choice into your prayer. If not, simply rest in having chosen. The bell holds the time.
Savitri and Satyavan. A princess too radiant to be asked, sent out to choose, who comes home with the name of an exiled king's son.
Your line: Savitri and Satyavan. Today, make one small choice fully your own, and notice how it feels to stand behind it. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

796.title: Savitri and Satyavan
796.hook: Narada praises the young man Savitri has chosen, then names his one flaw: he will die within a year
796.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, Narada's warning and Savitri's reply that she chooses only once both come before the wedding, so she marries Satyavan already knowing about the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday began the story of Savitri and Satyavan: a princess sent out to choose, who came home with the name of an exiled king's son. What choice did you stand behind? Day seven hundred ninety-six.

Savitri has just said his name, and the sage Narada says: oh no. He doesn't mean the young man is bad. Quite the opposite. Ashvapati asks him what's wrong with Satyavan, and Narada starts listing what's right. He's truthful. He's generous. He's patient, handsome, kind to everyone. Every good thing you could want. And then the sage stops, and says there's one flaw, and it outweighs all the rest. Here is the hinge of the whole story, said aloud at a royal court.
screen: `NARADA SAYS: OH NO.` → `EVERYTHING RIGHT ABOUT HIM.` → `AND ONE FLAW.`

segments.voice: The flaw is this, Narada says: a year from today, Satyavan will die. The court goes quiet. Her father turns to Savitri at once. Go, he says, choose someone else. And Savitri's answer is the center of today. In the telling, she says something like this: some things happen only once. A daughter is given in marriage once. A person says I give, once. I have chosen once. Whether his life is long or short, whether he is full of virtues or not, I have chosen my husband, and I won't choose twice. My mind decided first, then my words said it, and now I'll act on it. Look at the shape of what she says. She doesn't argue that Narada is wrong. She doesn't promise to fix it. She hears terrible news and keeps her word anyway, because to her, a choice of the heart is a promise already made. And Narada, the one who brought the bad news, doesn't argue with her. He tells the king: her mind is steady. Let it be. Then he blesses the marriage and goes. So Ashvapati travels into the forest to find old blind Dyumatsena under a tree. The exiled king is worried. We have lost our kingdom, he says. We live on what the forest gives. How could a princess bear this life? Ashvapati answers that his daughter already knows all of it. The two fathers agree. And Savitri is married to Satyavan, there among the hermitages, carrying a piece of news her husband doesn't know.
screen: `"A YEAR FROM TODAY."` · `"CHOOSE SOMEONE ELSE."` · `"I HAVE CHOSEN ONCE."` · then, large: `MARRIED IN THE FOREST, KNOWING.`

If you pray, you can bring that decision into your prayer. If not, simply rest with it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Savitri and Satyavan. A warning from Narada, a father's plea, and a daughter who says she has chosen once, and won't choose twice.

797.title: Savitri and Satyavan
797.hook: in the forest hermitage Savitri counts the days nobody else is counting, and takes a hard vow before the last one
797.howItsDone: In the epic, Savitri's three-night vow comes just before the day Narada foretold, and she keeps it standing and fasting without telling anyone why.

segments.voice: Yesterday the story of Savitri and Satyavan went on: a choice made, and a warning heard. Your line was Savitri and Satyavan. What did you hold to, even when it cost something? Day seven hundred ninety-seven.
screen: `SAVITRI AND SATYAVAN.` · `A CHOICE, AND A WARNING.`

segments.voice: A calendar, kept in one person's head. In the forest hermitage where Savitri now lives, nobody else is counting. Her husband Satyavan gathers fruit and splits wood. His father, a king who lost his sight and then his kingdom, lives there quietly with his wife. Savitri has put away her jewels and wears the rough clothing of the forest. She serves the old couple, and she speaks gently to everyone. And every day, she counts. Because she still carries the words the sage Narada spoke at her father's court: that Satyavan would not live out the year. She tells no one. In the epic, those words stay with her day and night. Today the days run short, and Savitri does something about it.
screen: `A HERMITAGE IN THE FOREST.` → `NARADA'S WORDS, KEPT SILENT.` → `SHE COUNTS THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: As the day draws close, Savitri takes a vow. The epic calls it the triratra, the three-night vow, and she keeps it standing, without food, day and night. Her father-in-law, Dyumatsena, is alarmed. He tells her the vow is too hard, close to unbearable. Savitri answers him gently. Don't grieve, father. I will finish it. It is resolve that carries a vow through. And the old king, blind and kind, gives way. I can't tell you to break it, he says. Keep it, then. Look at what she does, and what she doesn't do. She doesn't tell him why. She doesn't ask anyone to fix it. She doesn't run. She takes the dread she has carried alone and gives it a shape: a vow, with a beginning and an end, kept with her own body. A vow like this is a vrata: a promise kept with discipline, here with fasting, for someone loved. Tradition says steady discipline like this gathers tapas, a strength that comes from holding firm. Savitri isn't waiting for the day to fall on her. She is getting ready to meet it. On the last night she stands until morning. Then the day itself arrives. She makes her offerings to the fire, and the hermits bless her. The elders urge her to eat at last. Savitri says she'll eat when the sun goes down. The forest is going about its morning, and only one person in it knows what this day is.
screen: `THE THREE-NIGHT VOW, KEPT STANDING.` · `THE BLIND KING LETS HER KEEP IT.` · `DREAD GIVEN A SHAPE.` · then, large: `I'LL EAT WHEN THE SUN GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, or sit tall, the way Savitri keeps her vow. Feel your feet, or your seat, carrying your weight. Bring to mind one thing you've been carrying by yourself, a worry you haven't said out loud. Don't try to solve it. Just let it have a shape, with edges, the way Savitri gives her dread a beginning and an end. Breathe in, and feel the ground hold you. Breathe out, and stay steady. If you pray, you can hold that worry in your prayer. If not, simply stand with it, kindly. The bell holds the time.
Savitri and Satyavan. The wife who counts the days and keeps a hard vow standing, and the husband who doesn't yet know. Today's words.
Your line: Savitri and Satyavan. Today, take one thing you've been dreading and give it a shape: a time, a first step, an end. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

fork.reveal: she keeps the three-night vow, standing and fasting, and tells no one the reason. she's not waiting for the day; she's getting ready for it.

original.note: Sanskrit: a vow, often kept with fasting; Savitri's is a three-night one.

trapdoor: what you thought: Savitri just waits for the worst day of her life.

798.title: Savitri and Satyavan
798.hook: Savitri walks into the forest beside Satyavan on the day itself, and Death comes for him in person
798.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, Yama comes for Satyavan in person, draws out his life with a noose, and turns south, and Savitri follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri and Satyavan: Savitri kept the three-night vow standing, and said she would eat when the sun went down. Your line was Savitri and Satyavan. Did you give a worry a shape? Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

Satyavan shoulders his axe. He's heading into the woods for fruit and firewood, the way he does every morning. And Savitri, who has eaten nothing through her vow, asks to come along. He's surprised. You've never come with me before, he says, the path is hard, and you're weak from fasting. She won't be talked out of it. She even goes to his parents and asks their leave, and they give it. So the two of them set off together, and the epic says she looks cheerful while her heart is burning.
screen: `AN AXE AND A FOREST PATH.` → `SHE ASKS TO COME ALONG.` → `CHEERFUL, WITH A BURNING HEART.`

segments.voice: Satyavan shows her the forest as they walk, the streams and the flowering trees, and she answers him and watches him. He gathers fruit. He starts to split wood. And then he stops. His head aches, he says. His limbs hurt. He wants to lie down. Savitri sits on the ground and takes his head into her lap. And then she sees someone. A tall figure, dark, dressed in red, with a noose in his hand, standing over Satyavan and looking at him. Savitri lays her husband's head down gently, stands, joins her palms, and asks who he is. He tells her. He is Yama, the lord of death, and Satyavan's time has come. Then she asks a question you might not expect at a moment like this. Why have you come yourself? I'd heard your messengers do this work. Yama answers that Satyavan was good, and handsome, and full of virtue, and so he wasn't to be fetched by servants. Yama would come himself. And with his noose he draws out of Satyavan's body a person no bigger than a thumb. The body lies still. Yama turns and sets off toward the south. And Savitri follows. That's where the week leaves her: walking behind Death. Look back, and this week began with Nala and Damayanti and turned to Savitri. Two stories told to the exiled Pandavas in the forest, and in both, a woman who refuses to let go.
screen: `HIS HEAD IN HER LAP.` · `A DARK FIGURE WITH A NOOSE.` · `WHY HAVE YOU COME YOURSELF?` · then, large: `SAVITRI FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Rest one hand on your chest, the way Savitri holds Satyavan's head. Bring to mind someone you once looked after when they were sick or tired: a child, a parent, a friend. Remember the weight of it, the quiet of sitting with them. Breathe in, and let that care come back. Breathe out, and let it rest in your hand. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If not, just stay with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Savitri and Satyavan. His head in her lap, Death at the edge of the clearing, and Savitri standing up to speak to him. Today's words.
Your line: Savitri and Satyavan. Today, when someone close to you is tired, sit with them for a few minutes without trying to fix anything. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.
